segments.english: Rabbi Ishmael his son says: One who holds himself back from judging removes from himself enmity, robbery, and a false oath. But one who is overbold of heart in giving rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit.
segments.literal: Rabbi Ishmael his-son saying: the-holding-back himself from-the-judgment, removing from-him enmity and-robbery and-oath-of falsehood. And-the-coarse his-heart in-the-instruction, fool wicked and-coarse-of spirit.

tokens.note: participle: 'is saying'; the habitual present of a saying
a Qal participle with the article, 'the one who ...'; a subject clause
literally 'his bone', that is 'his own self'; the pack's lexicon entry for עֶצֶם is the place-name Ezem, which does not fit
הַדִּין, 'the judgment', here the work of sitting in judgment
פּוֹרֵק, literally 'unloads, takes off (a burden)'
שָׁוְא: an oath that is empty or false
גַּס, literally 'coarse, thick'; the pack's lexicon entry for גַּס I is 'falcon', which does not fit the sense
בַהוֹרָאָה, 'in the giving of legal instruction'; the pack has no usable lexicon text for הוֹרָאָה
גַּס רוּחַ is a fixed phrase for arrogance, coarseness of spirit

phrases.english: Rabbi Ishmael his son says
phrases.literal: 'Rabbi Ishmael his-son saying'; the son of the Rabbi Yose of the preceding mishnah, so Rabbeinu Yonah's heading

phrases.english: One who holds himself back from judging
phrases.literal: 'the-holding-back himself from-the-judgment'; Bartenura: where there is one greater than he, or he tells the parties to compromise

phrases.english: removes from himself enmity, robbery, and a false oath
phrases.literal: 'removing from-him enmity and-robbery and-oath-of falsehood'; Bartenura gives the reason for each of the three

phrases.english: But one who is overbold of heart in giving rulings
phrases.literal: 'and-the-coarse his-heart in-the-instruction'; Bartenura: without study and deliberation; Rambam: without awe or fear

phrases.english: is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit

grammar: הַחוֹשֵׂךְ and הַגַּס are articular participle and adjective used as subjects: 'the one who holds back', 'the one who is coarse'.
The first sentence gives a cause and its three results, enmity, robbery and a false oath; the second sets the opposite case, with three damning terms.
גַּס לִבּוֹ is a subject-predicate phrase: 'coarse of heart'; גַּס רוּחַ is a construct chain: 'coarse of spirit'.
Rabbi Ishmael is called 'his son': the son of Rabbi Yose in 4:6.
segments.note: Rabbi Ishmael 'his son' is, by Rabbeinu Yonah's heading, the son of Rabbi Yose in 4:6. Bartenura and Rambam give the sense of גַּס לִבּוֹ בַהוֹרָאָה as giving rulings without study or fear, and the English 'overbold' follows that; the literal sense is 'coarse of heart'. The pack's lexicon entries for גַּס I (falcon) and עֶצֶם (Ezem) do not match the words, and I have kept the data and noted the mismatch.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: one holds back where there is a greater person present, or tells the litigants to compromise.
Bartenura: whoever leaves the court as the losing party hates the judge, saying in his heart that the judge did not turn the case in his favor.
Bartenura: the judge might hold the innocent party liable, so that a robbery comes about through him.
Bartenura: the judge might impose an oath on one not liable to it and so bring about a false oath; or the tanna calls a lying oath 'an oath of falsehood'.
Bartenura: he rules 'without examination and without waiting', which gives 'overbold' for גַּס לִבּוֹ.
Rambam: 'his heart is coarse in rulings, emboldened to give rulings without awe and fear'.

apparatus: Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma reads 'Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose'; the pack's base text has only 'his son'.
Rabbeinu Yonah cites Deut 16:18-20 and the duty to judge, answered by 'where there are no other judges'.

segments.english: He used to say: Do not judge alone, for none judges alone but One. And do not say, "Accept my opinion," for they are permitted, and you are not.
segments.literal: He was saying: not be judging alone, for-not judging alone except one. And-not say: accept my-opinion, for-they permitted and-not you.

tokens.note: הָיָה with a participle gives the habitual past: 'he used to say'
תְּהִי, short jussive form of הָיָה
the participle דָּן is from דין; the pack's lexicon entry for דָּן is the name Dan, which does not fit
יְחִידִי, an adverbial use of the adjective 'solitary'
שֶׁאֵין, 'that there is not'
אֶחָד: 'One' read as the Holy One, blessed be He (Bartenura); a person would then not judge alone
קַבְּלוּ, Piel imperative plural: the colleagues are addressed
דַעְתִּי, 'my view, my judgment'
שֶׁהֵן, 'that they'; הֵן is the feminine/common plural pronoun used here for the colleagues
רַשָּׁאִין, 'having authority, entitled'

phrases.english: He used to say
phrases.literal: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר, the formula of the decisions

phrases.english: Do not judge alone
phrases.literal: 'not be judging alone'; a prohibition with the jussive

phrases.english: for none judges alone but One
phrases.literal: 'for-not judging alone except one'; One is the Holy One (Bartenura)

phrases.english: And do not say
Accept my opinion
phrases.literal: 'accept my-opinion', the words of the proud judge to his colleagues

phrases.english: for they are permitted, and you are not

grammar: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר is a past habitual: 'he used to say'.
אַל תְּהִי דָן is a prohibition made of אַל, the jussive of הָיָה and a participle.
שֶׁאֵין דָּן יְחִידִי אֶלָּא אֶחָד: 'there is none judging alone except One'; the play is on יְחִידִי and אֶחָד.
שֶׁהֵן רַשָּׁאִין: the word רַשַּׁאי is the Mishnaic adjective 'authorized'.
segments.note: 'None judges alone but One': Bartenura reads אֶחָד as the Holy One; the English keeps 'One' with a capital so the ambiguity of 'one man' is not lost. The pack's lexicon entry for דָּן is the name Dan, which does not fit the participle.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: even an expert who may judge alone should not, as a way of piety, unless the parties have accepted him; then he may.
Bartenura: 'One' is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is alone in His world.
Bartenura: 'do not say' to your colleagues who disagree with you.
Bartenura: 'accept my opinion' means 'I am an expert and could have judged without your joining'.
Bartenura: since you joined them with you, the ruling should be decided by the majority.

apparatus: Rabbeinu Yonah brings a second explanation of 'except One': the expert (mumhe) alone may judge, but others should not count themselves experts.

segments.english: Rabbi Jonathan says: Whoever fulfills the Torah from poverty will in the end fulfill it from wealth. And whoever neglects the Torah from wealth will in the end neglect it from poverty.
segments.literal: Rabbi Jonathan saying: every the-fulfilling the-Torah from-poverty, his-end to-fulfill-it from-wealth. And-every the-neglecting the-Torah from-wealth, his-end to-neglect-it from-poverty.

tokens.note: Piel participle with the article: 'the one who upholds, fulfills'; the pack's lexicon entry for קְיָם is 'decree', which does not fit the verb
the object marker has no English counterpart
מֵעֹנִי, 'out of poverty', that is, while poor
סוֹפוֹ, 'his end', that is 'in the end'
infinitive construct with a feminine suffix, 'to fulfill her'; Torah is feminine
מֵעשֶׁר: the pack's lexicon entry (a tithing verb) does not match; the noun is 'wealth'
Piel participle: 'makes void, cancels, leaves idle'
'to make her void'

phrases.english: Rabbi Jonathan says
Whoever fulfills the Torah from poverty
will in the end fulfill it from wealth
And whoever neglects the Torah from wealth
will in the end neglect it from poverty

grammar: The two halves are in chiastic parallel: fulfilling from poverty leads to fulfilling from wealth; neglecting from wealth leads to neglecting from poverty.
מֵעֹנִי and מֵעשֶׁר: the מִן is of the circumstance, 'out of'.
The suffix הָ on לְקַיְּמָהּ refers to the Torah, which is feminine.
סוֹפוֹ לְ + infinitive means 'his end is to ...', 'he will end by ...'.
segments.note: 'Fulfills' and 'neglects' are chosen from Bartenura and Rambam: studying Torah under the pressure of need, as against leaving it for the preoccupation of wealth. The pack's lexicon entries for קְיָם ('decree') and עָשַׂר (tithing verb) do not fit קִיֵּם and עֹשֶׁר.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: from poverty means he is pressed for food and leaves his work to engage in Torah.
Bartenura: from wealth means that for the abundance of money he must turn his heart one way and another and has no leisure for Torah.
Rambam (filed at 4:8): the Torah allowed an expert to judge alone; the mishnah warns only as a moral counsel; colleagues who disagree cannot be forced. It bears on 4:8, not on the words of 4:9.

Rambam: one who studies Torah in poverty will in the end study it in wealth, free of distraction; one who neglects it for the sake of abundance will become poor, and his trouble to find bread will cause his neglect.

apparatus: Variants: Vilna reads המקיים, מעוני, לקיימה, מעושר (twice) and מעוני; the base text has the short spellings. No difference of meaning.
Rabbeinu Yonah cites Prov 30:8, 'give me neither poverty nor riches'.

segments.english: Rabbi Meir says: Limit your business, and engage in the Torah. And be humble of spirit before every person. And if you neglect the Torah, you have many idle ones against you. And if you toil in the Torah, He has much reward to give you.
segments.literal: Rabbi Meir saying: be lessening in-business, and-occupy in-the-Torah. And-be low-of spirit before-every person. And-if you-neglected from-the-Torah, there-is to-you idle-ones many against-you. And-if you-toiled in-the-Torah, there-is to-him reward much to-give to-you.

tokens.note: הֱוֵי is the Mishnaic imperative of הָיָה
Piel participle, 'one who lessens'
עֵסֶק, 'occupation, trade'
עֲסֹק, imperative of עסק, 'occupy yourself with'
שְׁפַל, construct of the adjective 'low'
בִּפְנֵי, literally 'in the face of'
בָּטַלְתָּ, 'you have ceased, been idle'; the verb is used for stopping study
יֶשׁ, the Mishnaic form of יֵשׁ
בְטֵלִים: the commentators differ on who they are, see the note
כְנֶגְדָּךְ, 'opposite you, set over against you'
עָמַלְתָּ, 'you have labored'
יֶשׁ לוֹ, 'there is to him': the sentence turns from 'you' to the third person; the commentators read the subject as God
לִתֶּן, the infinitive construct of נתן with a dropped nun

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says
Limit your business
phrases.literal: 'be lessening in-business'; Bartenura: in trade and work

phrases.english: and engage in the Torah
And be humble of spirit before every person
And if you neglect the Torah
you have many idle ones against you
And if you toil in the Torah
He has much reward to give you
phrases.literal: 'there-is to-him reward much to-give to-you'; the commentators supply God as subject

grammar: הֱוֵי and וֶהֱוֵי are the Mishnaic imperatives of הָיָה; וַעֲסֹק is an imperative of עסק.
The two conditions are parallel: if you neglect, if you toil; the first result is 'you have' (לְךָ), the second 'he has' (לוֹ), a shift to the third person.
בְטֵלִים הַרְבֵּה is 'many idle ones'; הַרְבֵּה is a Hifil infinitive absolute used as an adverb or adjective.
יֶשׁ לוֹ ... לִתֶּן is 'he has ... to give': a possessive idiom with an infinitive.
segments.note: בְטֵלִים is kept as 'idle ones': Bartenura offers two readings, those who help make you idle, and the wicked and beasts who are idle, by whom the Holy One brings punishment. Rabbeinu Yonah has the second. The English keeps the plain word. 'He has' keeps the Hebrew shift to the third person; Bartenura reads God as the subject.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: reduce your trade and work, and let your main occupation be Torah.
Bartenura: be humble in order to learn even from one lesser than you in wisdom. Rambam reads it more widely, humble even with the great and the small.
Bartenura gives two readings: those who help to make you idle, or the idle wicked and beasts through whom the Holy One brings punishment. The English keeps the plain 'idle ones'.
Bartenura: He Himself pays your reward, not through a messenger; thus the measure of good exceeds the measure of punishment.
Rambam: reduce trade and persist in Torah, and be humble before every person as if he were greater than you; this is to flee from pride.

apparatus: Variants: Vilna reads ועסוק and ליתן; base וַעֲסֹק, לִתֶּן.
Bartenura's second reading of בְטֵלִים, and Rabbeinu Yonah's 'bears and lions idle from work', both rest on the sense 'those who are idle'.

segments.english: Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says: One who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate. And one who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser. Repentance and good deeds are like a shield before punishment. Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker says: Every assembly that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure.
segments.literal: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Jacob saying: the-doing commandment one, acquiring for-him advocate one. And-the-passing transgression one, acquiring for-him accuser one. Repentance and-deeds good, like-shield before-the-retribution. Rabbi Johanan the-sandal-maker saying: every assembly that-it for-name-of Heaven, its-end to-be-established. And-that-not-it for-name-of Heaven, not its-end to-be-established.

tokens.note: קוֹנֶה, 'buys, gets for himself'; the pack's lexicon entry for קָנָה is a place-name, which does not fit
the 'ethic dative' לוֹ
פְרַקְלִיט, from Greek paraklētos
הָעוֹבֵר, 'the one who crosses over', here 'commits'; the pack's sense is 'to pass over'
קַטֵּגוֹר, from Greek katēgoros; the pack has no lexicon text for it
כִּתְרִיס, 'like a (large) shield'; the pack has no lexicon text
הַפֻּרְעָנוּת, 'the retribution, the calamity'; the pack has no lexicon text
כְּנֵסִיָּה, 'a gathering, an assembly'
literally 'for the name of'
'Heaven' stands for God
סוֹפָהּ, 'her end', since כְּנֵסִיָּה is feminine
hitpael infinitive, 'to be established, to stand'
וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ, 'and that she is not'

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer son of Jacob says
One who performs one commandment
acquires for himself one advocate
And one who commits one transgression
acquires for himself one accuser
Repentance and good deeds
are like a shield before punishment
Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker says
Every assembly that is for the sake of Heaven
will in the end endure
And one that is not for the sake of Heaven
will not in the end endure

grammar: הָעוֹשֶׂה and הָעוֹבֵר are participles with the article used as subjects; קוֹנֶה לוֹ is the predicate.
פְרַקְלִיט and קַטֵּגוֹר are Greek loanwords (paraklētos, katēgoros); one speaks for, the other against.
תְּשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים is a short sentence without a verb: a nominal predicate with כ-.
With Rabbi Johanan the Sandal-maker the saying changes: the two halves differ by לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם and its negation.
segments.note: פְרַקְלִיט and קַטֵּגוֹר are rendered 'advocate' and 'accuser', following Bartenura's 'good intercessor' and 'evil intercessor' and Rambam's court setting before the ruler. פֻּרְעָנוּת is 'punishment'; Rambam says blows and diseases. The pack's lexicon entries for קָנָה, טוֹב and שֵׁם are proper names and do not fit; I have kept the data and noted the mismatch.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: פְרַקְלִיט is an angel who intercedes for good.
Bartenura: קַטֵּגוֹר is an intercessor for evil; the word comes from 'calling a quarrel', and its opposite סַנֵּגוֹר means 'hating a quarrel'.
Rambam: the פרקליט speaks well for a man before the ruler; the קטיגור informs against him to the king and seeks to put him to death.

apparatus: Variants: Vilna reads עבירה, קטיגור, הפורענות and להתקיים (twice); base spellings are the short forms.
Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma 4:13:4 is anchored here in error; it belongs to 4:13.

segments.english: Rabbi Eleazar son of Shammua says: Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, and the honor of your colleague like the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher like the reverence for Heaven.
segments.literal: Rabbi Eleazar son-of Shammua saying: let-be honor-of your-student dear on-you like-that-of-yours, and-honor-of your-colleague like-reverence-of your-teacher, and-reverence-of your-teacher like-reverence-of Heaven.

tokens.note: יְהִי, jussive of הָיָה
כְבוֹד in the construct
חָבִיב, 'beloved, precious'
כְּשֶׁלְּךָ, 'like that of yours': שֶׁל is the Mishnaic genitive particle
חָבֵר, 'companion, fellow student'
כְּמוֹרָא, 'like reverence of'
רַבְּךָ, 'your rabbi, your master'
מוֹרָא, 'fear, awe'

phrases.english: Rabbi Eleazar son of Shammua says
Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own
and the honor of your colleague like the reverence for your teacher
and the reverence for your teacher like the reverence for Heaven

grammar: יְהִי is the jussive of הָיָה: 'let ... be'.
The three clauses form a chain: the last term of each clause is the first term of the next (honor of your student, honor of your colleague, reverence of your teacher, reverence of Heaven).
כְּשֶׁלְּךָ uses the Mishnaic particle שֶׁל: 'like that of yours'.
שָׁמָיִם is spelled with a qamets in the pack (שָׁמָיִם), the usual form is שָׁמַיִם; the dual noun stands for God.
segments.note: The three comparisons increase in rank: student, colleague, teacher, Heaven. The decision on שָׁמַיִם, of God, is 'Heaven'. The commentators (Bartenura) bring a verse for each clause; see the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: Moses made Joshua his student equal to himself, saying 'choose us men'.
Bartenura: Aaron said to Moses 'Oh my lord', though Moses was his younger brother, and called him lord.
Bartenura: 'my lord Moses, destroy them': whoever rebels against your teacher rebels as if against the Holy One and deserves destruction.

apparatus: Variant: Vilna reads חבירך for חֲבֵרְךָ.
Bartenura's verses: Exod 17:9 (Moses to Joshua, 'choose us men'); Num 12:11 (Aaron to Moses, 'Oh my lord'); Num 11:28 (Joshua, 'my lord Moses, destroy them').
